articles.title: A Show That Lovingly Pokes Fun at Gen Z
articles.text:
A Show That Lovingly Pokes Fun at Gen Z
Culture and entertainment recommendations including Adults, Emmylou Harris, and more
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
Welcome back to The Daily’s Sunday culture edition, in which one Atlantic writer or editor reveals what’s keeping them entertained. Today’s special guest is Emma Williams, an associate editor who helps oversee the magazine’s social media and has also written about her home state of Texas.
Emma is a habitual rewatcher of Normal People, a show that she says has resonated with her differently over time. She also enjoys listening to her namesake Emmylou Harris, laughing over Adults episodes, and watching Hailee Catalano’s comforting cooking videos.
— Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor
The television show I’m most enjoying right now: The first scene of FX’s Adults tells you pretty much everything you need to know about the show: It’s crass, crude, absurd, and indulgently hilarious. Adults pokes fun at Gen Z without being judgmental or predictable, and it features some familiarly ridiculous plights. Maybe don’t watch it with your grandmother—but your spunky aunt is probably okay.
A quiet song that I love: I discovered the British DJ Fred Again when I was going down an NPR Tiny Desk Concert rabbit hole years ago. I was immediately struck by his talent—but over time, I have come to better appreciate the emotion he evokes through his performances. Even in his natural habitat, behind the DJ booth, Fred isn’t what you might normally expect from an EDM artist: He samples spoken-word poems, Zoom calls, and random internet videos to create songs that you can just as easily dance to as you can cry to.
I know I’m cheating a bit by saying that his entire Tiny Desk production is my favorite quiet song, but the fact that he was able to pull off an acoustic EDM performance is remarkable. To re-create the sound of electronic beats, he used the marimba, the vibraphone, and the piano; he also pounded and tapped on a desk and layered in his soft, husky voice. It is gentle, engrossing, and stupidly impressive.
 
 A loud song that I love: The first time I heard “Dance Yrself Clean,” by LCD Soundsystem, I was confused. My best friend played it for me, and by minute two, I was enjoying the song, but I could not comprehend how this hazy and somewhat repetitive tune could continue for another seven minutes and be as “life changing” as she had promised.
 
 Then I hit 3:05 on the track. I felt the ba-da-da-dum in my bones before James Murphy’s newly impassioned voice flooded through the speakers. This is now my song for any moment when I need to drown out my thoughts. Whether I’m going through a breakup, a bad day, or an existential crisis, I’ll put on “Dance Yrself Clean” and itch through the first three minutes, eagerly anticipating the rush of euphoria that hits after the beat drops.
 
 Years later, that same friend and I heard the song live. I have no idea whether we were crying or laughing or shouting, but I know we were dancing with abandon—and letting the music wash over us.
A cultural product I loved as a teenager and still love: I watched Normal People for the first time when I was 19, and I’ve rewatched it at least once a year every year since. I have never wavered in my fondness for it, but my reaction to the characters and storylines has evolved with time.
 
 When I first saw the show, based on Sally Rooney’s novel of the same name, I fell madly in love with Connell, barely registering that his cold avoidance of Marianne in public was wrong. I just thought he was broody and complicated; therefore, to my teenage mind, he was perfect and dreamy. I’m glad to say that I have moved past that (kind of), and I now find it difficult to watch his treatment of Marianne in the first few episodes.
 
 In my 20s, I resonate more with Marianne’s college arc. Specifically, her need to become the coolest, most stylish, most successful version of herself—even if it comes at the cost of her own happiness.
 
 Marianne and Connell’s lack of clear communication is always maddening. But I understand it more with age. Sometimes vocalizing what you really want can be more terrifying than staying quiet.
A musical artist who means a lot to me: I have to pay homage to my namesake, the inimitable country folk artist Emmylou Harris. Her music reminds me of my home state of Texas. Listening to her song “Boulder to Birmingham” transports me back to long drives through the plains of West Texas and the seemingly endless miles of wind turbines. I hear my parents’ voices, lovingly calling me Emmylou and Emmy-lou-lou. Whenever I feel adrift, her music pulls me back to the ground.
A YouTuber, TikToker, Twitch streamer, or other online creator I’m a fan of: I have an embarrassing confession: There is a cooking influencer whom I’m really obsessed with—as in, I went to a meet and greet of hers, and I send her the occasional tipsy Instagram DM. (Sometimes she even responds!)
 
 Hailee Catalano is a James Beard–winning chef. Her food is fresh and unique, and her video style isn’t gimmicky or aggressive like that of so many other cooking accounts—it’s simple and personable. My favorite series of hers is called Friday Night Dinner, which is a collaboration with her partner, Chuck Cruz, who is also a chef and content creator. They film themselves making a new meal every week, and I can only describe their vibe as homey. The videos sometimes have awkward pauses and funny asides (and, of course, clips of their dog, Gus), and watching them makes me feel like I’m sitting at the kitchen counter as two of my friends prepare something delicious for us to eat.
A poem, or line of poetry, that I return to: The older I get, the more I find myself recalling the lines of Langston Hughes’s poem “Harlem.” Hughes asks: “What happens to a dream deferred?” I recently turned 25, and the “quarter-life crisis” is certainly hitting me. I think about all of my childhood hopes that have dissipated, and all of the ones I still have that I’m not sure will come true. I, too, wonder what happens to these dreams.
Here are three Sunday reads from The Atlantic:
The Week Ahead
- Primetime, a crime thriller about the rise of the To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen and the world of televised vigilantism (in theaters Friday)
- Youth, a comedic-drama series about a 50-year-old divorcée balancing dating with caring for her aging parents and adult son (streaming today on HBO Max)
- Mazywood, a horror novel by Tananarive Due about a man uncovering the truth about his grandmother, set in Old Hollywood and the present day (out Tuesday)
Essay
Math Can’t Go On Like This
By Kai Williams
In late July, one of the world’s most famous mathematicians issued a warning to his field. Math is entering a “turbulent period,” the UCLA professor Terence Tao said in front of a packed lecture hall at the International Congress of Mathematicians. AI is getting so good at math, he said, that it’s causing a “crisis in our mathematical values and practices.”
Earlier in the same week that Tao gave his talk at math’s most prestigious conference, a researcher at Anthropic had used Claude to disprove an 87-year-old math conjecture. Still, when I asked mathematicians at the conference about their experiences with AI, most hadn’t thought deeply about the topic. Many seemed a little surprised that a journalist was asking them about it at all.
More in Culture
Catch Up on The Atlantic
Photo Album
Willem de Kooning took the language of drawing, ripped it up, and rearranged it, Sebastian Smee writes. Take a look at some of his drawings from a new exhibition about the influential abstract expressionist—and read about what he had to unlearn.

articles.title: Lâm Đồng công bố tình huống khẩn cấp về thiên tai tại khu dân cư hơn 450 người
articles.text:
Ngày 20/9, UBND tỉnh Lâm Đồng có Quyết định công bố tình huống khẩn cấp về thiên tai tại thôn Đắk Snao, xã Quảng Sơn do tình trạng sạt lở, sụt lún đất diễn biến phức tạp và đe dọa an toàn của hàng trăm người dân.
Cụ thể, từ ngày 1/9 đến 18/9, tình trạng sụt lún, sạt trượt đất tại thôn Đắk Snao ảnh hưởng trực tiếp đến 79 hộ với 454 nhân khẩu. Khu vực bị ảnh hưởng có diện tích hơn 4ha, nền đất sụt lún trung bình khoảng 20cm.
Dọc sườn đồi và khu dân cư xuất hiện nhiều đường nứt đất kéo dài khoảng 300m, rộng từ 6-17cm. Các vết nứt diễn biến nhanh, có xu hướng tiếp tục mở rộng. UBND tỉnh đánh giá nền đất tại khu vực đang có dấu hiệu mất ổn định nghiêm trọng.
Theo UBND tỉnh Lâm Đồng, nếu tiếp tục xảy ra mưa lớn hoặc mưa cường độ cao, nước thấm sâu có thể làm gia tăng nguy cơ sạt trượt, sụp đổ đất đá trên diện rộng, trực tiếp uy hiếp tính mạng, sức khỏe và nhà ở của người dân trong khu vực.
UBND tỉnh Lâm Đồng yêu cầu xã Quảng Sơn theo dõi chặt chẽ diễn biến thời tiết, khu vực sạt lở và vùng lân cận; đồng thời cắm biển cảnh báo, căng dây, bố trí lực lượng canh gác, hướng dẫn người dân không đi vào khu vực nguy hiểm; rà soát, vận động và tổ chức di dời người dân ra khỏi khu vực có nguy cơ.
Trường hợp tổ chức, cá nhân không tự giác chấp hành việc sơ tán, địa phương tổ chức cưỡng chế sơ tán theo quy định. Cùng với đó, các hộ phải di dời được yêu cầu bảo đảm đời sống và có phương án tái định cư phù hợp.
UBND tỉnh Lâm Đồng giao UBND xã Quảng Sơn rà soát quỹ đất, đề xuất xây dựng khu tái định cư trong trường hợp không thể xử lý khu vực sạt trượt hiện tại. Vị trí tái định cư phải bảo đảm ổn định địa chất, không có nguy cơ sạt trượt, thuận tiện cho học sinh đến trường và nhận được sự đồng thuận của đa số hộ dân bị ảnh hưởng.
UBND tỉnh Lâm Đồng giao Ban Quản lý dự án đầu tư xây dựng số 3 chủ trì, phối hợp với UBND xã Quảng Sơn và các đơn vị liên quan khảo sát, đánh giá chuyên sâu về địa chất, nguyên nhân và mức độ sạt trượt tại khu dân cư thôn Đắk Snao. Trên cơ sở kết quả đánh giá, đơn vị này đề xuất phương án xử lý lâu dài.
Sở Xây dựng tỉnh Lâm Đồng có trách nhiệm hướng dẫn quá trình đánh giá địa chất, nguyên nhân, mức độ sạt trượt và tham gia hướng dẫn địa phương trong trường hợp phải xây dựng khu tái định cư mới.
UBND tỉnh Lâm Đồng cũng yêu cầu huy động nguồn lực để xử lý khẩn cấp sự cố, triển khai khu tạm cư, cung cấp nhu yếu phẩm thiết yếu và không để người dân thiếu thốn trong thời gian sơ tán.

articles.title: TP.HCM: Nam thanh niên ngã xe tử vong trên đường Mỹ Phước Tân Vạn
articles.text:
Gần 1h ngày 20/9, Công an TP.HCM vẫn đang khám nghiệm hiện trường, điều tra nguyên nhân vụ nam thanh niên (chưa rõ danh tính) tử vong sau khi ngã xe máy trên đường Mỹ Phước Tân Vạn.
Theo thông tin ban đầu, hơn 21h ngày 19/9, người dân nghe tiếng động mạnh trên đường Mỹ Phước Tân Vạn, đoạn gần giao lộ với đường Bùi Thị Xuân (phường Tân Đông Hiệp).
Khi chạy ra kiểm tra, người dân thấy một nam thanh niên nằm bất động giữa đường, bên cạnh là chiếc xe máy mang biển số 60B9-742.09.
Nhận tin báo, Công an phường Tân Đông Hiệp phối hợp Đội CSGT Rạch Chiếc (PC08, Công an TP.HCM) đến hiện trường, lấy lời khai nhân chứng và trích xuất hình ảnh từ camera để xác định nguyên nhân vụ việc.
Công an đang tiếp tục điều tra, làm rõ vụ tai nạn.

articles.title: Guatemala’s Democracy Dilemma
articles.text:
Guatemala’s Democracy Dilemma
A reformist president weighs the pressure to move fast against the imperative to restore institutions his people can trust.
Just over three years ago in Guatemala, a coalition of young and Indigenous voters helped propel Bernardo Arévalo, a reformer who campaigned against corruption, to an astounding presidential win. Guatemala had not only refused the global trend toward populist authoritarianism; it had also defied what its citizens called “the pact of the corrupt,” a loose alliance of politicians, judges, criminal networks, and crony capitalists that had gained control of the country’s institutions.
Today the mood in Guatemala is less hopeful. Some of Arévalo’s former allies, and many of those who voted for him, are dejected, convinced that the president missed a once-in-a-generation opportunity to transform the country. When I met with Arévalo in Guatemala City in May, he defended the pace of his administration’s progress and suggested that the alternative would have been to abuse the powers of a government he was elected to reform.
In Latin America, “we never truly got used to understanding that the rule of law is fundamental,” he told me. “Rule of law is not the same as rule by law. Rule of law is when we all accept that we are subject to the law and we operate within that framework to solve problems. Rule by law is when I use the law that’s at my disposal as part of my political arsenal.”
Had he crossed that line, Arévalo insisted, he would have risked being ousted by his opponents and replaced by someone willing to do much worse. His critics disagree.
Arévalo’s personal integrity is undisputed. But some of the reformers who helped elect him now argue that he may be too scrupulously rules-respecting to deal effectively with the “pact of the corrupt” and the institutions it captured—too much of a liberal democrat to save democracy. When he leaves office in 2028, they fear that the pact will quickly retake control of the few institutions it has lost, or that voters will choose an autocrat who promises to crush crime without concern for legality.
Guatemala’s predicament points to a more universal problem. Can liberal reformers unwind authoritarian state capture without, themselves, engaging in at least a little bit of illiberalism? The dilemma is not Guatemala’s alone. Move too aggressively, and you risk being branded an autocrat, or even becoming one. Move too cautiously, and you risk obstruction, sabotage, and ineffectuality. South Africa’s Cyril Ramaphosa chose a gradualist approach to reversing Jacob Zuma’s state capture and disappointed many of his supporters. Placing the opposite bet, Poland’s Donald Tusk bent rules to try to undo the damage done by the right-populist Law and Justice party—and stood accused of undermining the rule of law. Hungary’s post-Orbán leader, Péter Magyar, seems to be following Tusk’s example.
In a way, both Arévalo and his critics are right. Guatemala has avoided a democratic breakdown. But the president’s rules-bound approach has also left many Guatemalans feeling that he has not fought for them forcefully enough. The question now is whether Arévalo has preserved democracy as an ideal that Guatemalans believe in and, if necessary, will defend.
In Guatemala City, I watched as hundreds of people gathered outside the country’s public prosecutor’s office, a bunker-like building ringed by a huge black-steel fence put up three years before, allegedly to shield the occupants from nonviolent democracy protesters. The crowd had come to celebrate the long-awaited end to the term of María Consuelo Porras, the country’s attorney general and, to many citizens, the personification of the pact of the corrupt.
For the past eight years, Porras had been a figure of fear. She used the power of her position to investigate and jail critics of state corruption. When Arévalo was elected in 2023, her office tried to overturn the results, alleging irregularities that international observers found baseless. That effort looked likely to succeed—until indigenous Maya communities organized peaceful demonstrations that lasted 106 days and drew the participation of nearly 2 million Guatemalans. Arévalo was inaugurated.
That he did not take extralegal action to remove Porras from her post has given rise to some of the fiercest criticism against him. She opened an investigation into Arévalo’s party, the Seed Movement, for relatively minor party-registration irregularities. Although the probe did not produce formal charges, it led to the party’s dissolution and thus thwarted any hope of its controlling Congress. Porras also brought more than 75 legal cases or complaints against the president and his supporters, including the arrests of two of the Indigenous leaders behind the 2023 protests, and even a cabinet minister. Now Porras was finally leaving, and a new attorney general was taking over.
The Guatemalans gathered outside the office had waited for this moment. What they had not anticipated was how long Porras’s departure would take, and how few people would come out to celebrate it. Thousands had massed in the same street just a few years before.
When I met Arévalo a few days later, he justified the delay by explaining that his government had arrived “with an enormous level of public legitimacy, but without control of the Congress, and with the justice system positioned against us.”
Legally, he had no authority to simply eject the attorney general. He sent a bill to Congress to grant him that power, but the opposition blocked it. “If, in that scenario, I make a political miscalculation, the result isn’t that I go with a hundred people to pull Consuelo Porras out of that building and that this is sustainable and produces results,” he said. It was that “I go to prison or into exile, and someone else comes in, one of them, to take power.”
Like much else in Guatemala, the colossal, mint-green presidential palace where Arévalo sat down with me is a holdover from a bygone era of authoritarianism. It was built by Guatemala’s Hitler-admiring, yet U.S.-backed dictator, Jorge Ubico, who rose to power in 1931 and was forced to resign amid mass protests in 1944.
Arévalo, before winning the presidency, was best known as the son of the man who succeeded Ubico, in Guatemala’s first truly free elections. Juan José Arévalo, an educator and a social democrat, returned to Guatemala from exile in 1944 to run for president against the ex-dictator’s favored candidate. As his son would later, he won by a landslide, and Guatemala’s “democratic spring” began, a time of expanded rights and education. But after his freely and fairly elected successor, Jacobo Arbenz, went further, carrying out a land reform that threatened the interests of wealthy families and the powerful U.S.-based United Fruit Company, the United States organized a coup that put the military in power in 1954. Nine years later, a guerrilla leader asked Arévalo to help spearhead armed resistance to the regime, and the former president refused, saying that confronting the military head-on would turn Guatemala “into a lake of blood.”
He was right. In the name of crushing the greatly outnumbered guerrillas, the military and its allies killed or disappeared more than 100,000 Guatemalans over the next three decades. It massacred leftists, labor leaders, and residents of more than 400 Maya villages suspected of supporting insurgents. Guatemalan courts eventually deemed the latter crime a genocide.
Bernardo Arévalo, born in exile in Uruguay, returned with his family in the middle of the dictatorship period, and he began a career as a diplomat at its tail end, as the country formally returned to elections and civilian rule in 1985. He later left the diplomatic service, earned a Ph.D., and worked in international peace-building.
The wood-paneled presidential office where we met was decorated only with two portraits: his father’s, in black-and-white, and his own, beside it, in color. Arévalo’s demeanor was professorial.
“We are in a process of recovery,” he said. “Democracy doesn’t develop in a linear, unidirectional way; it has leaps and twists, not only here, but everywhere in the world.” For much of the 1990s and 2000s, Guatemala had been twisting its way toward democracy, but corruption networks and drug traffickers had insinuated themselves into the country’s institutions. “Part of what we set out to do is to recognize the serious damage this had caused the country—this corrosion, this penetration of political-criminal networks” that served no “ideological interest,” Arévalo said, but rather “the highest bidder: whoever could pay for impunity.”
Dislodging these forces from the machinery of the state has been neither swift nor straightforward, and even those most anxious for change are hard-pressed to offer practical solutions. The president told me that some supporters had asked him to use the military to remove Porras. He found the suggestion unsettling: “Are you really asking us to go back to the years of military dictatorships of the 1970s, when armies were the only solution?”
I asked Arévalo about the Indigenous protest leaders, Luis Pacheco and Hector Chaclán, who had then been imprisoned for more than a year while under investigation on terrorism charges. “I would like the people who say ‘But the government could have done something else’ to tell me what,” Arévalo replied, exasperated. “What they’re venting is the frustration we all feel.”
He assured me that the pact of the corrupt was weakening incrementally as its networks lost access to the state: first the executive branch, then the public-works contracting system, now the prosecutor’s office. “Without tools, they aren’t powerful. And our task is to keep removing those tools from them.”
Arévalo can point to some successes. Young lawyers have worked to clean up corruption in the judicial selection process. Appointed in March, the new bench of the Constitutional Court, which rules on the constitutionality of laws and policies, is more favorable to reformers than the one it replaced, as is the new electoral tribunal, which oversees elections. I spoke with the new attorney general a few days after he assumed his post: He was so busy firing Porras’s apparatchiks and preparing for the institution to resume serious criminal investigations that he was sleeping only four or five hours a night. An anti-corruption commission that Arévalo formed early on has already filed more than 200 criminal complaints against former officials.
Arévalo was tasked with not only freeing a state captured by kleptocrats, but also strengthening one that was fundamentally weak. The bureaucracy he inherited had little capacity to provide public services, reduce poverty, or fight organized crime. In this, too, his administration has made some progress. It has hired more than 15,000 new teachers, and built or refurbished more than 150 rural-health clinics (his predecessor built just six in four years, Arévalo said). The government has also replaced dirt floors with cement in more than 75,000 households in the country’s poorest rural municipalities, and has distributed water filters and cleaner-burning stoves.
Still, much else that Guatemalans had hoped for has failed to materialize. Congress, which remains dominated by the old-guard pact forces, has blocked or stalled bills aimed at curbing corruption—for example, bills to modernize public-works contracting, require shell companies to disclose who owns them, and protect whistleblowers. Partly because the contracting system remains dysfunctional, the government has made little visible progress toward repairing the country’s crumbling highways. And, unwilling to buy votes in Congress outright, as his predecessors did, Arévalo has resorted to pork-barrel spending and raising congressional salaries to win legislative support. Such tactics are deeply unpopular with the public.
Another limiting factor has been the Trump administration. Although Arévalo’s cooperation on crime and drugs has kept the relationship cordial, his opponents have courted President Trump to try to tip the scales against reformers. In April, the U.S. ambassador to Guatemala personally called reluctant Guatemalan lawmakers to pressure them to approve a Constitutional Court judge favored by pact elites and conservatives, a top lawmaker, Luis Aguirre, told me. This tied the court between reformers and their opponents, leaving Arévalo without a reliable majority.
The young reformers who campaigned with Arévalo knew that he would face constraints, but some wish that he had more often tested those limits.
Samuel Pérez, 34, is a member of Congress; he was also the head of the Seed Movement bloc in Congress before it was dissolved. I went to see him in a building plastered with missing-persons flyers for those who were disappeared during the military dictatorship decades ago. The flyers are a common sight in Guatemala City, posted and reposted by the victims’ families.
Pérez told me that Arévalo was elected not only “to overthrow the regime, but also to construct something new, and that isn’t happening.” Now Pérez was creating a party, called Raíces, to which most of the lawmakers formerly associated with the Seed Movement had defected. They would still support Arévalo, but they would advocate for a more confrontational approach. “The president interprets power and good government as doing things a little better and a little more than what already existed. For me, no. You don’t use power to administrate what’s already there, but to transform what isn’t working,” Pérez explained.
I’d last seen Pérez during Arévalo’s presidential campaign in 2023. He’d told me then that if the Seed Movement won, the government’s greatest difficulty would be managing popular expectations. But he hadn’t predicted that he himself would be among the disappointed. Arévalo should have rallied the public to pressure Congress to pass the law removing Porras, Pérez said. He should have conceded less to business elites, and done more to free Pacheco and Chaclán. Pérez was particularly upset that the police had come to arrest the two men in a white van with tinted windows—a symbol of the dictatorship, which used such vehicles to disappear its victims—and that the government had not stopped this.
Several young Guatemalans in the reform movement suggested to me that the political caution of their parents’ generation was a product of the fear instilled in them during the years of military rule and internal armed conflict. Some speculated that Arévalo’s aversion to escalation emanates from that experience, too, given his youth in exile and the persecution of many of his father’s supporters in the years after the 1954 coup. “I think he is a son of his circumstances,” said Andrea Reyes, a young lawmaker helping Raíces organize.
Arévalo readily locates his most formative influences in that era—as a source not of fear, but of strengthened conviction. He spoke to me of his father’s refusal to abandon democratic principles: “Even when the world began to change around him, he kept his convictions, which today we see were the correct convictions, after all, 80 years later.”
Arévalo, too, has found his convictions under pressure—not only from former allies who worry that his reforms have gone too slowly, but also from constituents and conservative politicians who want a government that will ignore constitutional limits in cracking down on crime. In this they compare him unfavorably with the autocrat next door: Many Guatemalans who live in daily fear of extortion and kidnapping see gangs, not illiberal state capture, as the biggest threat to their basic freedoms, and they see President Nayib Bukele’s El Salvador as a beacon of safety.
Bukele, first elected in 2019, took an almost opposite approach from Arévalo’s to governing. He purged institutions of his political rivals, packed them with loyalists, and then cut secret deals with gang leaders before cracking down on their followers. His mass roundups virtually eliminated violent crime in his country, by jailing more than 90,000 people suspected of gang ties, many without due process. Arévalo is unwilling to pursue such methods. He has, however, seized record quantities of cocaine, extradited crime bosses, hired thousands of new police officers, and begun building the country’s first new maximum-security prison in 40 years. But murder and extortion rates have proved stubborn, and many are now demanding more-radical methods.
“Guatemalans are searching for their Bukele,” said Alvaro Arzú Escobar, a conservative lawmaker sanctioned by the Biden administration for allegedly trying to undermine Arévalo’s inauguration. Arévalo “isn’t radical in his ideas or his actions,” Arzú told me. But, he added, “the country’s biggest problem right now is a lack of authority. As president, he doesn’t exercise the power he holds. There is a lot of rhetoric, but little action.”
The Mariscal Zavala military prison sits on a pine-covered ridge on the outskirts of Guatemala City. A former army base, it houses the state’s highest-profile prisoners. I went there to meet Pacheco and Chaclán, the Indigenous leaders who’d played such an instrumental role in safeguarding the 2023 presidential election. Both had been on the board of the 48 Cantones of Totonicapán—one of the country’s oldest Indigenous self-governing bodies, in rural western Guatemala—when the attorney general’s office had moved to annul the vote. Pacheco and Chaclán canvassed rural villages on foot, helping gather some 50,000 signatures calling for Porras’s resignation. Later they helped organize protests in the capital.
“The 48 Cantones is also a democracy, with elected leaders and term limits,” Chaclán told me. “For us, democracy is sacred, and although Guatemala often doesn’t reflect it much, we must respect it.”
In April 2025, Porras ordered him and Pacheco into pretrial detention. After that, their court hearings were repeatedly delayed, seemingly intentionally, and when I met them in May, they had no idea when the next one would be.
I asked them whether they believed Arévalo should have rallied protesters or found some other tool to remove Porras, and thus to free them. Pacheco responded, “I would have liked it at first, but later I realized it would have only changed the person, not the form of doing justice.” Chaclán added, “This is nothing simple, and surely he is doing what is best for the country. We have faith we have already passed the majority of our time here.”
Chaclán was right. On August 5, a judge released Pacheco and Chaclán to house arrest, reuniting them with their families. Around the same time, the prison-like, black-steel fence was taken down from around the public prosecutor’s office.
Guatemala’s next presidential election is just nine months away. Right-wing candidates are beginning to emerge, some imitating Bukele, and many sure to court the White House, in the hope that Trump will try to tip the scales. Arévalo’s and Pérez’s reformists claim that they will join forces behind a unity candidate, but such a figure has not yet surfaced. Democracy is twisting its way forward, in Arévalo’s words. No one thinks it is leaping.
But the passage of time may provide a different perspective. On one of my last days in Guatemala City, I walked by a cathedral I had passed dozens of times before. I had never previously noticed the tiny engraved names of more than 13,000 victims of the internal armed conflict, so small as to be illegible from even a short distance, on its stone columns.
For much of the 20th century, Guatemalans who advocated for self-government, equality before the law, and the welfare of the majority—that is, social democrats—knew that the state might try to kill them. Today, social democrats govern. Reformers may disagree as to whether Bernardo Arévalo made the most of the opportunity he was given. But that such an opportunity could ever arise is more than many members of his father’s generation likely thought possible.
*Image Sources: Luis Soto / AP; Johan Ordonez / AFP / Getty; Arnulfo Franco / AFP / Getty.

articles.title: Xác minh clip 'thầy trò Đường Tăng' cưỡi ngựa trên làn ô tô ở TPHCM
articles.text:
Ngày 20/9, mạng xã hội lan truyền clip ghi lại cảnh một nhóm người hóa trang thành các nhân vật trong phim Tây Du Ký di chuyển vào làn đường dành cho ô tô, gây mất an toàn giao thông.
Qua tìm hiểu, vụ việc xảy ra trên đường Phan Văn Khải, đoạn qua xã Tân An Hội, TPHCM.
Hình ảnh từ clip cho thấy nhóm 4 người hóa trang thành Tôn Ngộ Không, Sa Tăng, Trư Bát Giới và Đường Tăng. Trong đó, người đóng vai Đường Tăng cưỡi ngựa trắng, 3 người còn lại đi bộ trên làn đường dành cho xe container, ô tô tải theo hướng từ Tây Ninh đi TPHCM.
Thời điểm xảy ra vụ việc, lượng phương tiện lưu thông trên tuyến đường khá đông. Một số tài xế xe tải, xe đầu kéo phải chủ động giảm tốc độ, điều khiển phương tiện tránh nhóm người để đảm bảo an toàn.
Sau khi được đăng tải, đoạn clip nhận nhiều bình luận từ cộng đồng mạng. Nhiều ý kiến cho rằng việc cưỡi ngựa, đi bộ vào làn đường dành cho xe cơ giới, trong điều kiện phương tiện lưu thông đông, tiềm ẩn nhiều nguy cơ xảy ra tai nạn giao thông.
Cơ quan chức năng đang xác minh thời điểm và diễn biến vụ việc để xử lý theo quy định pháp luật.

articles.title: Xe tập lái gây cản trở giao thông, xử lý thế nào?
articles.text:
Hỏi: Tôi tham gia giao thông và nhận thấy tại một số tuyến đường vẫn còn tình trạng xe tập lái cố tình chạy chậm hoặc bám một làn gây cản trở các xe khác. Vậy, cần làm gì để các xe tập lái này lưu thông có văn hóa hơn?
Chu Văn Hiếu (Bắc Ninh)
Đại diện Cục CSGT (Bộ Công an) trả lời:
Thời gian vừa qua, qua theo dõi tình hình trật tự, an toàn giao thông và phản ánh của người dân, Cục CSGT nhận thấy tại một số tuyến đường vẫn còn tình trạng xe tập lái chưa chấp hành nghiêm các quy định của pháp luật về trật tự, an toàn giao thông.
Một trong những nguyên nhân của tình trạng trên là do nhiều giáo viên dạy lái xe chưa nhận thức đúng về ý thức và đạo đức của người lái xe. Điều này dẫn đến họ hướng dẫn học viên đi đường chưa có văn hóa giao thông (điển hình là việc chạy chậm bám trái…).
Xe tập lái vi phạm không chỉ gây cản trở giao thông, tiềm ẩn nguy cơ ùn tắc, tai nạn giao thông mà còn có thể hình thành thói quen tham gia giao thông không đúng quy định cho người học lái xe.
Để chủ động phòng ngừa, hạn chế nguy cơ xảy ra tai nạn liên quan đến xe tập lái, Cục CSGT đã đề nghị Cục Đường bộ Việt Nam nhiều nội dung.
Theo đó, cần quán triệt các cơ sở đào tạo lái xe thực hiện nghiêm quy định pháp luật về trật tự, an toàn giao thông trong quá trình đào tạo thực hành trên đường; nâng cao trách nhiệm của giáo viên dạy thực hành, tăng cường hướng dẫn, giám sát học viên, đặc biệt khi tập lái trên các tuyến đường có tốc độ, mật độ phương tiện cao.
Bên cạnh đó, thường xuyên kiểm tra, rà soát hoạt động đào tạo thực hành; kịp thời chấn chỉnh, xem xét xử lý hoặc kiến nghị cơ quan có thẩm quyền xử lý đối với các trường hợp vi phạm nhiều lần, vi phạm nghiêm trọng, bảo đảm tính nghiêm minh và sức răn đe.
Thời gian tới, lực lượng CSGT toàn quốc tiếp tục tăng cường tuần tra kiểm soát, kịp thời phát hiện, xử lý nghiêm các hành vi vi phạm của xe tập lái trong quá trình tham gia giao thông.

articles.title: 190 Days Without a Homicide
articles.text:
Jenee Gragston dropped to the ground and held on to the grass as if it could save her life. She yelled to her family members to get down. She later told me that she didn’t know where the bullets were coming from, but she knew they were close. When the firing stopped, the cries began. She could hear her 4-year-old nephew howling: “Get it off me! Get it off me!” She wasn’t close enough to see what had happened, but it looked like he had blood on his chest. A teenage boy was lying near the child. The teenager “never screamed or anything,” she said. “I can still see all of it.”
It was a Saturday afternoon, mid-August in Lexington, Kentucky. Hundreds of people had gathered in Charles Young Park to celebrate what’s called East End Day—a combination of family reunions, live music, and lots of food. I grew up going to festivals in that park, though I lived on the west side of town, in the Charlotte Court housing projects.
Kentucky isn’t the most dangerous place in America, but it’s up there, with the 14th-highest rate of gun deaths. Twelve years ago, my uncle was murdered in Lexington. Three years ago, my sister’s husband was shot and killed there. I worry about my brother, who still lives there. He had gotten himself off the streets for a while, but is now back living in the city. Lexington had recently seen a hard-won drop in gun deaths—last year was the fourth straight year of declines in gun violence among young people. This spring and summer set a record of 190 straight days without a homicide. Then came the East End Day shooting, which killed that teenager, 16-year-old Di’Zhon Robertson, and wounded four others—including the 4-year-old, who was shot in the leg. The next weekend, another person was killed. The weekend after that, four separate shootings left two more dead.
Gragston was selling Polish sausages in the park. She’d paid more than $300 for the grill, $300 for the sausages, more than $1,000 in fees, $75 for the booth. Business was good; some people returned for seconds. Her husband, her kids, and other family members had come to help her set up her tent. Her 4-year-old nephew was handing customers sodas and water bottles. On the basketball court nearby, Devine Carama was talking with a group of young people. Carama is the director of ONE Lexington, a city-funded program that tries to prevent gun violence by mentoring at-risk boys. He, too, threw himself down when he heard gunfire. “I almost got shot that day,” he told me. Two people near him were hit—a man and his girlfriend. Carama and others tried to bandage the man’s leg; he told me he could see a glimmer of bullet or bone through the blood.
A day later, 18-year-old Jametrius Griffin turned himself in and was charged with murder. According to court testimony, Griffin’s younger brother had gotten into an argument; punches were thrown, and the younger brother fell or was pushed. When Griffin saw that, he yanked out a gun and started firing.
For the past three years, Robertson had participated in ONE Lexington’s summer youth program, which offers workshops on building emotional and social skills, as well as college-campus visits. “He wasn’t a street kid,” Carama said. Griffin’s younger brother was in ONE Lexington, too—in its school mentoring program. The organization had also helped Griffin get a job at UPS. The group’s work seemed to be making a difference. And then a fight left one young man dead, one wounded, and one in prison.
In many ways, Lexington feels like a small town, where everyone knows everyone. I went to middle school with Griffin’s lawyer, Daniel Whitley, who has a big reputation locally for representing people accused of murder—and for winning their cases. The week after the shooting, I spoke with Whitley and with Griffin’s mother, Jay-Me Baxter, on a video call.
“A bunch of bullshit” was how Baxter described the park shooting, “because everybody’s friends and everybody’s family.” She said her youngest son told her he had been bullied by Di’Zhon Robertson and others. The day after the shooting, she made the same argument in a video she posted on Facebook that outraged many in the community. She suggested that her older son had had no choice and said she didn’t care “who makes it home as long as mine do.” (I tried to reach Robertson’s mother through family members to see if she would talk with me about what happened to her son; her sister replied that the family didn’t want to relive it. But friends and family members described the teenager as quiet, observant, and “very respectful.”)
“I’m like, Shit, I know Di’Zhon’s mama,’” Baxter told me—the other mother was close friends with her own sister. Baxter said she had had a conversation with her about the beef between the boys, and assumed the issue had been settled. Griffin loved football, and he had started college at Kentucky State University. “But you know them kids,” she said. “They be doing stuff in silence.” Her son must have been simmering with fury.
I knew Baxter’s family growing up—she’s a year older than me, and they, too, lived in the Charlotte Court housing projects. She didn’t remember me, but she knew my brother. Her mother was white, and had nine children. Baxter, the third-oldest, is half Black, like her younger siblings. But the oldest two are white. Her mother used to cry, Baxter told me, because “the white kids didn’t ever live with us.” In our majority-Black neighborhood, a white mother with mixed-race kids stood out. Baxter remembers people throwing rocks through their windows and a lot of name-calling—“white bitch.” Her family was poorer than many others, but people in the neighborhood assumed that she was privileged, and tormented her for it. “That white mama, man,” she said. “You know what I’m saying?”
That kind of bullying is part of the pain of being impoverished. You feel so low, you desperately want to make someone else feel lower.
Baxter is a single mother, and Griffin is the oldest of her five children. Like my own mother, she lost custody of her kids because of drugs—she signed over her parental rights to her mom. She told me the story as if she was discussing a character in a book: “Jay-Me got in trouble. Jay-Me started using drugs, cocaine specifically.” Like my mother, Baxter was a victim of sexual abuse. She grew up watching her mother “get beat by men. I done been touched by men, and I never told my mama until a couple months before she died.”
It took Baxter seven years to stop using drugs and get her kids back. Those kids needed her, yet she kept choosing drugs over them, she said, as her voice cracked and tears hit her cheeks. “That hurts, because I can’t believe I did that.” I’ve heard those same words from my own mother and watched her cry for the same reason.
Before Baxter signed over her rights, she said, she asked her mother to promise that what she’d experienced as a little girl wouldn’t happen to her kids. She wanted to break the cycle of violence, poverty, and dysfunction that is the inheritance of so many children. “I’m not a gun mama,” Baxter told me, but she believes in “stepping in the street” to fight. “I’ve been fighting all my life,” she said.
Backgrounds like these are so common in Whitley’s line of work that he seemed to tune out our conversation. At one point on the video call, we heard the sound of snoring. Baxter joked about it: “Listen to him. My lawyer tiiiiiired.” We continued talking for a few more minutes and never heard from him again. “Night night, Daniel,” she said before we hung up. He called me back later, apologized for not saying goodbye, and said he hadn’t been asleep.
Despite the pity I felt for Baxter and her family, I felt more for those shot by her son, and their families.
Di’Zhon Robertson’s uncle Tyrone Johnson officiated his funeral, and told me that the church was full of people “struggling with their emotions.” I was told by attendees that the teenager’s grieving mother had to be pulled off the coffin. Damon Williams Jr., a 14-year-old wounded in the shooting, was hit in the thigh. He had been planning on joining his middle school’s football team this season. Lakeisha Martin was shot in the stomach and the sternum. East End Day, her older brother Isaiah Barron told me, “is a day for our community that we look forward to every year.” Martin was in the hospital for 21 days and will be unable to work for months.
The day of the shooting, Jenee Gragston rushed to the hospital as her nephew went into surgery. She told me the police said she should leave her tent, and could return later to retrieve everything. But when her husband went back to the park, almost everything was gone. The cooler with the meat. The grill, the propane tank, even her prescription eyeglasses. Other tents had been robbed as well. Gragston told me that she was grateful her nephew was okay, but that she would never go to one of the park festivals again.
Lexington is trying hard to reduce this kind of gun violence. Mayor Linda Gorton told me the city has handed out free gun locks and offered to buy back guns from residents, among other interventions. Through ONE Lexington, it offers groceries, hotel stays, and educational funds to people affected by gun violence. The city relocated a family whose house had been shot up, Gorton said. Still, she conceded, “there are times when we cannot control every human being’s behavior.”
It doesn’t help that Kentucky has such lax gun laws. Just this year, state legislators dropped the age required to carry a concealed firearm from 21 to 18. When I was growing up in Lexington, gun violence was even worse. Whenever you have a community of young men who feel powerless and disrespected, who have been raised to protect themselves and their families from perceived threats, and who believe words can’t save them but a gun might, then death will follow. The story of what happened in Lexington this summer is particularly tragic because so many had worked so long and so carefully to make a difference. But a gun changes everything in a moment.
Carama, of ONE Lexington, told me he has more friends who are dead than alive. He, too, said that “a lot of it is out of our control,” and that there’s only so much someone from outside a young person’s family can do. You can monitor a kid all you like, but if he has a gun, “you got a split second to react.” Ultimately, he said, “you can’t prevent everything. It’s just not possible.”
In Jay-Me Baxter’s account, she tried, in her way, to intervene. “The mamas grew up together,” she told me. “This could’ve been prevented.” But it wasn’t.

articles.title: 4 cội nguồn sức mạnh của Houthi và hướng tấn công tiếp theo
articles.text:
Ngày 19/9, Ảrập Xêút xác nhận lực lượng phòng không nước này đánh chặn một tên lửa đạn đạo hướng vào Riyadh, AP đưa tin. Đây là lần đầu tiên thủ đô Ảrập Xêút trở thành mục tiêu kể từ khi vòng xung đột mới bùng phát.
Cùng thời điểm, Ảrập Xêút cho biết Houthi tìm cách tấn công cơ sở hạ tầng tại Yanbu, Taif và Baysh. Houthi tuyên bố đã sử dụng phối hợp tên lửa đạn đạo, tên lửa hành trình và máy bay không người lái (UAV).
Điều đáng chú ý là đây không còn đơn thuần là những cuộc tập kích xuyên biên giới từ Yemen. Vài tuần qua, Houthi đã đồng thời mở rộng kiểm soát lãnh thổ ở bờ Biển Đỏ, tiến tới Bab el-Mandeb và gia tăng sức ép lên các tuyến vận tải cũng như cơ sở năng lượng của Ảrập Xêút.
Không chỉ tên lửa, Houthi có cả một hệ sinh thái chiến tranh
Một trong những lý do khiến Houthi trở nên khó đánh bại là họ không phụ thuộc vào một loại vũ khí duy nhất.
Theo các đánh giá gần đây, lực lượng này sở hữu hỗn hợp tên lửa đạn đạo, tên lửa hành trình, UAV, vũ khí chống hạm và phương tiện không người lái trên biển. Một số hệ thống có nguồn gốc hoặc chịu ảnh hưởng công nghệ Iran, trong khi Houthi ngày càng có khả năng tự sản xuất và cải tiến một phần vũ khí tự tạo, theo AP.
Điều này tạo ra một bài toán rất khó cho Ảrập Xêút: để ngăn chặn một cuộc tấn công, Riyadh phải đối phó nhiều lớp mối đe dọa khác nhau, trong khi mỗi UAV giá tương đối thấp có thể buộc bên phòng thủ sử dụng một tên lửa đánh chặn đắt tiền.
Đó chính là logic của chiến tranh bất đối xứng: Houthi không nhất thiết phải phá hủy hoàn toàn một mục tiêu để đạt hiệu quả. Chỉ cần khiến hệ thống phòng thủ phải liên tục hoạt động, làm gián đoạn hàng không, hàng hải, năng lượng và tạo tâm lý bất an là họ đã tạo ra sức ép chiến lược.
Địa hình Yemen biến Houthi thành mục tiêu cực kỳ khó diệt
Houthi hoạt động trên một không gian rộng lớn với những vùng núi hiểm trở của Yemen. Các cơ sở quân sự, kho vũ khí và lực lượng có thể được phân tán, khiến ưu thế không quân của Ảrập Xêút khó chuyển hóa thành một chiến thắng trên mặt đất.
Đây là bài học mà Ảrập Xêút đã trải qua trong cuộc chiến bắt đầu từ năm 2015.
Suốt nhiều năm, không quân Ảrập Xêút cùng lực lượng đồng minh không kích quy mô lớn nhưng không thể loại bỏ Houthi. Các chuyên gia nhận định rằng, muốn đánh bại hoàn toàn lực lượng này, cần có lực lượng mặt đất đủ mạnh để kiểm soát lãnh thổ sau các cuộc không kích. Nhưng chính lực lượng chống Houthi tại Yemen lại bị phân mảnh sâu sắc.
Nói cách khác, Houthi không chỉ mạnh lên vì họ có thêm vũ khí. Đối thủ của họ cũng chưa hình thành được một lực lượng mặt đất thống nhất đủ sức tận dụng những khoảng trống do không kích tạo ra.
Iran cung cấp đòn bẩy công nghệ nhưng Houthi không hoàn toàn là “con rối”
Một cách giải thích đơn giản là coi Houthi chỉ như “cánh tay nối dài của Iran”. Thực tế phức tạp hơn.
Iran được cho là đã cung cấp cho Houthi đào tạo, công nghệ và các thành phần vũ khí tiên tiến. Các chuyên gia và báo cáo quốc tế cũng ghi nhận những mối liên hệ quân sự giữa Houthi với Iran và các lực lượng đồng minh của Tehran. Iran phủ nhận việc cung cấp vũ khí vi phạm lệnh cấm vận.
Nhưng Houthi có động cơ riêng. Theo Viện Nghiên cứu quốc tế Hoàng gia Anh (Chatham House), lợi ích của Houthi và Iran thường giao nhau nhưng không hoàn toàn trùng nhau. Với Houthi, gây sức ép trên Biển Đỏ vừa có ý nghĩa trong cuộc cạnh tranh khu vực, vừa giúp họ củng cố vị thế chính trị trong nội bộ Yemen và chứng minh khả năng đối đầu với những cường quốc quân sự mạnh hơn.
Đây là điểm rất quan trọng khi dự đoán bước đi tiếp theo: không nên giả định rằng mọi quyết định quân sự của Houthi đều do Tehran trực tiếp chỉ đạo.
Houthi đã có thêm bàn đạp chiến lược ở Biển Đỏ
Bước ngoặt lớn nhất trong tháng 9 không nằm ở một quả tên lửa nhằm vào Riyadh mà nằm ở bản đồ.
Houthi đã chiếm thành phố Mokha, sau đó tiến xuống khu vực eo biển chiến lược Bab el-Mandeb và kiểm soát đảo Perim, theo các báo cáo được Hội đồng Quan hệ đối ngoại (một tổ chức nghiên cứu độc lập của Mỹ) tổng hợp. Điều này đưa Houthi đến gần một trong những điểm nghẽn hàng hải quan trọng nhất thế giới.
Chatham House đánh giá việc Houthi kiểm soát Mokha và tiến sát Bab el-Mandeb là thay đổi lãnh thổ có ý nghĩa nhất trong nhiều năm của cuộc chiến Yemen.
Và đây là lúc sức mạnh của Houthi vượt ra ngoài phạm vi Yemen. Eo biển Hormuz nằm trong vòng ảnh hưởng của Iran, còn Bab el-Mandeb đang chịu sức ép từ Houthi.
Hai điểm nghẽn này nằm ở hai đầu của mạng lưới vận tải năng lượng và thương mại kết nối Trung Đông với châu Âu và châu Á. Vì vậy, một lực lượng không có không quân hay hải quân theo nghĩa truyền thống vẫn có thể gây tác động lớn đến kinh tế toàn cầu.
Houthi sẽ tấn công mục tiêu nào tiếp theo?
Không thể biết chắc mục tiêu tiếp theo của Houthi, và những tuyên bố về các mục tiêu đã bị đánh trúng hiện vẫn có những điểm chưa thể kiểm chứng độc lập. Nhưng nếu nhìn vào mẫu hình hoạt động hiện nay, có thể nhận diện một số hướng phát triển ở cấp độ chiến lược.
Khả năng cao nhất là Houthi tiếp tục mở rộng sức ép lên hạ tầng năng lượng và giao thông của Ảrập Xêút. Đây là hướng đã xuất hiện rõ trong những tuần gần đây.
Houthi đã tuyên bố tấn công các cơ sở năng lượng Ảrập Xêút; Riyadh cũng xác nhận nhiều cuộc tập kích nhằm vào các địa điểm trong nước. Ngày 19/9, Ảrập Xêút cho biết Houthi tìm cách tấn công Yanbu - nơi có một tuyến đường ống dầu quan trọng đấu nối - bên cạnh Riyadh và một số địa điểm khác.
Vì thế, về mặt chiến lược, cơ sở năng lượng, cảng biển và mạng lưới vận tải nhiều khả năng tiếp tục nằm trong vùng nguy hiểm.
Mục tiêu của kiểu chiến dịch này không nhất thiết là phá hủy toàn bộ ngành dầu khí Ảrập Xêút. Chỉ cần gây gián đoạn hoặc làm tăng đáng kể chi phí bảo vệ và vận chuyển, Houthi đã tạo được hiệu ứng kinh tế và tâm lý.
Khả năng cao nhì là Riyadh có thể tiếp tục bị đặt dưới sức ép. Cuộc tấn công ngày 19/9 cho thấy Houthi đã nâng cấp đáng kể thông điệp chiến lược: không còn chỉ nhằm vào khu vực biên giới phía Nam Ảrập Xêút mà có thể đe dọa cả trung tâm quyền lực của vương quốc.
Ảrập Xêút nói tên lửa hướng tới Riyadh đã bị đánh chặn và không có thương vong hay thiệt hại được báo cáo. Houthi lại tuyên bố đã đánh vào các “mục tiêu nhạy cảm”. Hai phiên bản này chưa hoàn toàn thống nhất và một số tuyên bố của Houthi chưa được xác minh độc lập.
Do đó, có thể dự đoán áp lực lên Riyadh sẽ tiếp tục, nhưng không nhất thiết dưới dạng những đợt tấn công liên tục vào khu vực đô thị. Điều đáng chú ý hơn là khả năng Houthi duy trì mối đe dọa đủ lớn để buộc Ảrập Xêút phải phân tán nguồn lực phòng không trên phạm vi rộng.
Khả năng cao ba là mở mặt trận thứ hai trên Biển Đỏ. Đây có lẽ mới là hướng có ý nghĩa chiến lược lớn nhất.
Sau khi tiến tới Mokha và Bab el-Mandeb, Houthi có khả năng sử dụng vị trí địa lý mới để gây sức ép lên tàu hàng và tàu liên quan Ảrập Xêút, đồng thời đe dọa tuyến vận tải qua Biển Đỏ.
Chatham House nhận định, chiến thuật của Houthi trên biển không cần phải đánh chìm hàng loạt tàu. Chỉ cần tạo đủ bất định để các hãng tàu đổi tuyến, phí bảo hiểm tăng và các chính phủ phải bỏ thêm nguồn lực bảo vệ hàng hải, hiệu ứng kinh tế đã rất lớn.
Đây là một dạng chiến tranh mà một lực lượng tương đối nhỏ có thể tạo ra chi phí rất lớn cho đối thủ.
Điểm yếu của Houthi
Nhưng Houthi cũng đang đứng trước một giới hạn rất rõ. Sức mạnh của Houthi không đồng nghĩa với khả năng chiến thắng không giới hạn.
Thứ nhất, lực lượng này vẫn phụ thuộc vào Iran đối với một số công nghệ và linh kiện quân sự tiên tiến.
Thứ hai, chiến dịch càng mở rộng, nguy cơ Ảrập Xêút và các đối tác quốc tế hình thành một hệ thống phòng thủ chung càng lớn.
Thứ ba, việc Houthi tiến xuống eo biển Bab el-Mandeb cũng khiến họ trở thành mục tiêu quân sự quan trọng hơn đối với nhiều nước có lợi ích trực tiếp trong tự do hàng hải.
Và đặc biệt, Ảrập Xêút hiện được cho là đang tìm kiếm hỗ trợ phòng không từ Pháp, Anh, Pakistan và Ai Cập trong bối cảnh nguồn tên lửa đánh chặn chịu áp lực.
Điều này tạo ra một nghịch lý: Houthi càng đánh mạnh, họ càng chứng minh được sức mạnh; nhưng càng đánh mạnh, họ càng tạo động lực để một liên minh rộng hơn hình thành chống lại mình.
Một cuộc chiến “rẻ để tấn công, đắt để phòng thủ”
Nếu phải tóm tắt cội nguồn sức mạnh Houthi trong một công thức, đó sẽ là: địa hình Yemen + lực lượng đông đảo + vũ khí giá tương đối thấp + công nghệ tên lửa/UAV + hỗ trợ từ Iran + khả năng tự sản xuất + đối thủ bị phân mảnh + vị trí địa lý tại eo biển Bab el-Mandeb.
AP dẫn nguồn tin nói rằng, số lượng nhân lực Houthi có thể đã tăng từ khoảng 30.000 năm 2015 lên khoảng 350.000 vào năm 2024. Trong khi đó, các chiến dịch không kích của Mỹ và đồng minh trước đây đã gây thiệt hại đáng kể nhưng không thể triệt tiêu lực lượng này.
Vì vậy, hướng phát triển đáng chú ý nhất trong thời gian tới có lẽ không phải là một đòn đánh quyết định duy nhất. Đó có thể là một chiến lược bào mòn nhiều tầng: gây sức ép lên Ảrập Xêút từ trên không, đe dọa hạ tầng năng lượng, duy trì rủi ro đối với hàng hải ở Biển Đỏ và đồng thời củng cố vị trí trên bờ Yemen.
Nếu mô hình này tiếp tục, cuộc chiến sẽ ngày càng ít giống một cuộc xung đột Yemen - Ảrập Xêút truyền thống và ngày càng giống một cuộc đấu tranh kiểm soát các nút thắt chiến lược của Trung Đông, trong đó eo biển Bab el-Mandeb trở thành quân bài đặc biệt quan trọng.
Houthi mạnh khi đánh phân tán, ẩn trong địa hình, dùng vũ khí tương đối rẻ, buộc đối phương phòng thủ, tận dụng sự chia rẽ của đối thủ. Lực lượng này yếu dần khi phải giữ lãnh thổ rộng, bảo vệ tuyến hậu cần dài, duy trì lực lượng ven biển, bị giám sát liên tục, phải đối phó nhiều lực lượng thống nhất, chịu áp lực chính trị trong các vùng mới chiếm.
Vì thế, kịch bản khó khăn nhất đối với Houthi không nhất thiết là một cuộc tổng tấn công của Ảrập Xêút. Nó có thể là một chiến dịch kiên trì khiến họ phải cùng lúc bảo vệ quá nhiều thứ.
Và đây cũng chính là nghịch lý của chiến thắng Houthi tháng 9/2026: việc họ tiến đến eo biển Bab el-Mandeb làm tăng đáng kể quyền lực chiến lược của họ, nhưng đồng thời cũng biến họ thành một mục tiêu dễ bị quốc tế hóa và dễ bị bao vây hơn.
Nếu xu hướng hiện nay tiếp diễn, cuộc đấu giữa Riyadh và Houthi vì thế có thể chuyển từ ai có nhiều tên lửa hơn sang một câu hỏi khó hơn nhiều: ai có khả năng duy trì chiến tranh lâu hơn mà không làm đứt gãy hậu cần, liên minh và nền tảng chính trị của chính mình?
Tổng quan sức mạnh của Houthi
Houthi tại Yemen đã phát triển thành một lực lượng quân sự hùng mạnh và độc lập, có khả năng thách thức các quốc gia trong khu vực và gây gián đoạn các tuyến đường hàng hải toàn cầu, hãng tin Đức DW nhận định.
Năng lực quân sự và kho vũ khí:
-Vũ khí hiện đại: Lực lượng Houthi sở hữu kho vũ khí đồ sộ gồm tên lửa đạn đạo, tên lửa hành trình chống hạm và UAV với năng lực sánh ngang các quốc gia hiện đại.
-Sản xuất tại chỗ: Với sự hỗ trợ từ các kỹ sư Iran và các linh kiện nhập lậu, Houthi đã phát triển năng lực tự lắp ráp, chế tạo các loại UAV giá rẻ (một số chỉ tốn khoảng 1.500 USD) và cải tiến tên lửa ngay tại địa phương.
-Vị trí chiến lược: Những bước tiến gần đây dọc theo bờ biển Biển Đỏ, bao gồm các khu vực gần eo biển Bab al-Mandeb, mang lại cho Houthi lợi thế trực tiếp trong việc kiểm soát các tuyến đường thương mại quốc tế và vận chuyển năng lượng huyết mạch toàn cầu.
Lợi thế chiến lược và tính độc lập:
-Khả năng chống chịu bất đối xứng: Khác với các nhóm khác trong khu vực, Houthi không hoạt động trong hệ thống tài chính quốc tế và không phải duy trì cơ sở hạ tầng phúc lợi dân sự trong nước, khiến các biện pháp trừng phạt kinh tế hay việc phá hủy cơ sở hạ tầng hầu như không mang lại hiệu quả.
-Quyết tâm ý thức hệ cao độ: Việc đề cao tinh thần hy sinh và tử vì đạo khiến các biện pháp răn đe quân sự thông thường hay các cuộc không kích trả đũa đều thất bại trong việc bẻ gãy ý chí chính trị hoặc quyết tâm hành động của Houthi.
-Tính độc lập trong tác chiến: Mặc dù liên kết với “trục kháng chiến” của Iran, Houthi vẫn duy trì mức độ tự chủ cao, theo đuổi các mục tiêu riêng tại địa phương và khu vực ngay cả khi những mục tiêu này khác biệt so với sự kiểm soát chặt chẽ từ phía Tehran.

articles.title: Cận cảnh tuyến đường 100 tỷ đồng ở Quảng Trị bị sạt lở, hư hỏng nặng sau mưa lũ
articles.text:
Giao thông Đường bộ Cận cảnh tuyến đường 100 tỷ đồng ở Quảng Trị bị sạt lở, hư hỏng nặng sau mưa lũ Duy Lợi - 20/09/2026, 06:09 Tuyến đường nối xã Trường Ninh với xã Trường Sơn (Quảng Trị) bị sạt lở nhiều vị trí trong đợt mưa lớn vừa qua. Đây cũng là đoạn thuộc tuyến nối đường Hồ Chí Minh nhánh Đông với đường Hồ Chí Minh nhánh Tây đến trung tâm xã Trường Sơn. Ngày 19/9, lãnh đạo UBND xã Trường Sơn (tỉnh Quảng Trị) cho biết, địa phương đang phối hợp với Ban QLDA Đầu tư xây dựng xã Quảng Ninh và các đơn vị liên quan để tiến hành kiểm tra, đánh giá các vị trí bị sạt lở, hư hỏng do đợt mưa lớn vừa qua trên tuyến đường nối xã Trường Sơn với xã Trường Ninh.Video: Cận cảnh tuyến đường 100 tỷ đồng ở Quảng Trị bị sạt lở cùng những tảng đá lớn rơi xuống, cây "khủng" bật gốc chắn ngang.Ghi nhận của PV Báo Xây dựng, do ảnh hưởng của đợt mưa lớn vừa qua, đoạn tuyến dài 6,5km thuộc tuyến đường kết nối giao thông gần nhất từ xã biên giới Trường Sơn về xã Trường Ninh có nhiều vị trí bị sạt lở, hư hỏng nặng.Đây cũng là đoạn thuộc tuyến đường huyết mạch nối đường Hồ Chí Minh nhánh Đông đoạn qua xã Trường Xuân, huyện Quảng Ninh cũ (hiện nay là xã Trường Ninh) với đường Hồ Chí Minh nhánh Tây đến trung tâm xã Trường Sơn.Điểm đầu đoạn tuyến 6,5km thuộc dự án vừa hoàn thành giai đoạn 1 và đã được bàn giao đưa vào sử dụng vào tháng 6/2026, nằm tiếp giáp với tuyến đường nối từ đường Hồ Chí Minh nhánh Đông đoạn phía Nam cầu Long Đại thuộc xã Trường Ninh lên.Từ đây di chuyển hơn 1km có hai vị trí đất đá từ ta luy dương sụt xuống gần nhau, trong đó một vị trí đất đá tràn ra nửa đường. Vị trí còn lại đất đá án ngữ toàn bộ mặt đường, nền đường và rãnh thoát nước dọc bị xói lở nặng.Đoạn tuyến còn lại chủ yếu uốn lượn “bên núi, bên vực” qua rừng tự nhiên, nhiều vị trí ta luy dương đất, đá bị sụt trượt tràn xuống mặt đường, ta luy âm xói lở. Ngoài đá nhỏ còn có nhiều tảng đá lớn lăn xuống đường do sạt lở.Trên tuyến, cây cối gãy đổ chắn ngang hoặc nằm lơ lửng phía ta luy dương, có cả cây cổ thụ đường kính “khủng” đã khô cũng ngã xuống nằm chắn ngang toàn tuyến.Tại một số vị trí, nước chảy qua cuốn theo đất đá, nền đường xói lở thành rãnh sâu.Có đoạn nền đường tiếp tục bị sạt ra phía ta luy âm và sụt xuống, ăn sâu vào khoảng 1/2 mặt đường.Ông Hoàng Mạnh Hà, Chủ tịch UBND xã Trường Sơn cho biết, tuyến đường nối Trường Ninh với xã Trường Sơn đưa vào sử dụng giai đoạn 1 đã bước đầu phát huy hiệu quả kết nối giao thông, giúp người dân xã “miền ngược” Trường Sơn về đường Hồ Chí Minh nhánh Đông, rút ngắn hơn 30km so với di chuyển đường vòng qua QL9E, QL9B về “miền xuôi”; hoặc phải đi thuyền qua sông.Tuyến đường nói trên thuộc dự án Đường cứu hộ, cứu nạn xã Trường Xuân, huyện Quảng Ninh cũ (hiện nay là xã Trường Ninh) đi xã Trường Sơn - giai đoạn 1, được UBND tỉnh phê duyệt vào tháng 7/2021, với chiều dài khoảng 6,5km, nền đường rộng 7,5m, mặt đường rộng 5,5m tổng mức đầu tư 100 tỷ đồng từ nguồn vốn ngân sách Trung ương.Dự án giai đoạn 1 với nền đường cấp phối, các công trình thoát nước ngang và cầu trên tuyến đã hoàn thành và được bàn giao đưa vào sử dụng hồi tháng 6 vừa qua. Hiện, thời tiết diễn biến phức tạp, tuyến đường vẫn đang tạm thời cấm lưu thông tại các vị trí nguy hiểm.Chính quyền xã Trường Sơn đã chủ động liên hệ, phối hợp với Ban QLDA Đầu tư xây dựng và Phát triển quỹ đất xã Quảng Ninh (chủ đầu tư) để kiểm tra, đánh giá các vị trí sạt lở, hư hỏng nhằm sớm khôi phục giao thông và bảo đảm an toàn cho người dân.Theo Ban QLDA Đầu tư xây dựng xã Quảng Ninh, dự án vẫn trong thời hạn bảo hành, Ban sẽ phối hợp với các đơn vị liên quan và UBND xã Trường Sơn khảo sát thực tế, đánh giá để xử lý, khắc phục các vị trí sạt lở, hư hỏng do đợt mưa lớn vừa qua. Xã Trường Sơn cũng kiến nghị tỉnh bố trí nguồn vốn để sớm triển khai giai đoạn 2 nhằm cứng hóa mặt đường và hoàn thiện các hạng mục.Quảng Trị: Mưa lớn, nhiều cầu tràn ngập sâu, 59 hộ dân được di dời đến nơi an toànMưa lớn, nước sông dâng cao, 59 hộ dân khu vực bị ngập lụt tại xã Lao Bảo (Quảng Trị) đã được di dời đến nơi an toàn; nhiều cầu tràn, ngầm tràn tại một số xã miền núi phía Tây Nam tỉnh đang bị ngập sâu.

articles.title: The Firebrand
articles.text:
The Firebrand
Abdul El-Sayed wants to win the Michigan Senate race his way—as an unabashed progressive populist and a fierce critic of Israel.
Updated at 2:50 p.m. ET on September 20, 2026
Abdul El-Sayed certainly enjoys an argument. Our first interview, in a kebab restaurant in Dearborn, Michigan, spun out into a wide-ranging discussion of America’s Middle East policy, and ended with me saying, reluctantly, “Well, let’s not relitigate the Six-Day War.”
El-Sayed is campaigning to be the next Democratic senator from Michigan, but he has also become one of his party’s leading critics of Israel. I had observed that Gaza’s Arab neighbors had shown little desire to help Palestinians escape the humanitarian crisis there; he had retorted that without Israel’s bombing campaign, they wouldn’t need sanctuary in the first place. But we had run out of time. With a week to go until the primary, his schedule was packed, and his team needed to get him to the next event. He exited the restaurant, bestowing clouds of back slaps, handshakes, shukrans, and habibis on the staff. The former means “thank you” in Arabic; the latter, coming from El-Sayed, is probably best translated as “bro.”
The 41-year-old is not one of those hypercautious candidates who acts as though they’re carrying a Ming vase across a slippery floor, and he is not content to let Donald Trump’s unpopularity carry the Democrats to victory in November. His campaign is a crucial test of what kind of Democrat can prosper in a swing state. Michigan is deeply purple: It voted for Trump in 2016 and 2024, but its governor and two senators are Democrats. That makes El-Sayed the great hope for the Bernie Sanders wing of the Democratic Party—an anti-establishment economic populist running against, basically, Big Everything. He is also a Muslim, the child of Egyptian immigrants, at a time when Republicans are more and more comfortable saying that Islam is incompatible with Western values. During the Democratic primary, which El-Sayed won much more narrowly than polls had predicted, he campaigned alongside the Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, known for his admiration of Mao Zedong and the Soviet Union, and for saying that “America deserved 9/11.”
Voters on the left and the right regularly say that they want candidates who are fighters: In this environment, El-Sayed’s scrappiness should be an asset. He is willing to go into hostile territory, such as Jesse Watters’s Fox News show, and to call his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, a “beta” and “Mike Dodger” for refusing to debate him. But El-Sayed does not always pick his fights carefully. “He’s an empath,” says Brittany Huckabee, who made a documentary about him in 2018, “but he steels himself with this protective armor, almost like a bully—which serves him well in some ways, but I think it also alienates some people.”
That B-word also came up unprompted in my conversation with Monica Marks, an academic who knew him when they were both Rhodes Scholars at Oxford. “He doesn’t see himself as a bully,” Marks told me. “He sees himself as a bullier of bullies.” She thinks of him as a mixture of “serious intellectual” and “stubborn street fighter.” As an Arab American, El-Sayed faces the same challenge that Black politicians have long struggled to negotiate: What might look like passion in a white candidate is interpreted instead as aggression. Mehdi Hasan, who founded the left-wing online news start-up Zeteo, contrasted the Senate nominee’s political persona with that of New York City’s smiley and charming mayor, Zohran Mamdani. “I put him more in my camp,” Hasan said of El-Sayed. “We have RAMF: resting angry Muslim face.” As a result, half of the Republican attacks on El-Sayed paint him as a rabid Islamist who wants to institute Sharia law. (The other half imply that he’s a cheesy and effete Millennial, another Democratic soy boy clowning for the camera.)
For El-Sayed, though, having an argument is the point of running in the first place. He told me that merely holding the Senate seat for the Democrats was not the goal. “Using the seat is the goal,” he said, and mollifying opponents would therefore be fruitless. “So what would be the point of saying a bunch of things I don’t believe in, to avoid them spending money on me, to hold the seat—not to be able to do the things I want to do with it?”
El-Sayed says he gets his combative nature from his parents. His father, Mohamed, is an immigrant success story who moved from Egypt to pursue a doctorate in engineering at Wayne State University, in Detroit, and is now a professor at Eastern Michigan University. His mother, Fatten, was a medical student when the couple met. “Both are strong-willed, charismatic, charming—and both are uncompromising, not only in their beliefs, but also in their approaches to life and their way of doing things,” El-Sayed wrote in his 2020 memoir, Healing Politics. They divorced after his birth: “I comfort myself by thinking that if my parents were a band, they would have been a ‘one-hit wonder.’”
The young Abdulrahman—as he was then known—was raised by his father and his second wife, Jackie, “a distant descendant of Abigail Adams.” In one of his campaign ads, Jackie’s mother jokingly scolds him for saying the word heck. (Another ad spot features the uplifting strains of Journey’s “Don’t Stop Believin’,” described by one commentator as the “white people’s national anthem.”) At school, he was a jock and a nerd: captain of his high school’s football, lacrosse, and wrestling teams, as well as a high-scoring student who went on to study biology and political science at the University of Michigan.
The teenage Abdulrahman was also aware of being a child of two cultures. He traveled to Alexandria, in northern Egypt, during one summer vacation and saw how poverty, corruption, and state repression affected his cousins. “My grandmother used to remind me, like, you have nothing over any of your cousins except for: You get to go back to America at the end of the summer,” he told me.
In Egypt, according to his memoir, he got into trouble for shouting rude Arabic words about the dictator Hosni Mubarak, and was saved by his grandfather brandishing the teenager’s American passport at the police. (Another argument it might have been wiser not to start.) He writes that back in the United States, after 9/11, he got called racial epithets during football games, and once delivered an uppercut to an opposing player in response. “Son, let me tell you something: You’re going to be Abdul El-Sayed for the rest of your life,” he records his coach telling him. “You can either use it as an excuse or you can use it as motivation.” His half brother had it worse; his name is Osama.
During his early days in politics, El-Sayed used to grouse about comparisons being drawn between him and Barack Obama. But reading El-Sayed’s memoir, or talking with him now, you can see the beats borrowed from the former president: gratitude for America, and a desire for it to be better. “I’ve been able to live an amazing life because of what America gave me,” El-Sayed told me in Dearborn. “And also, I have watched as America has systematically denied that for too many people.”
As a junior at the University of Michigan, he met and proposed to a freshman named Sarah Jukaku. They married when she was a sophomore, although they didn’t live together at first. Jukaku is now a psychiatrist, and the couple have two young daughters. Jukaku joined us for lunch in Dearborn, where she worried that her light-gray hijab was a poor choice for a meal that leaned heavily on finger foods. When I asked how she felt about the possibility of becoming part of the most famous Muslim family in America, she shook her head. “I speak for myself here,” El-Sayed interjected before turning to her and saying, “Sarah, feel free to jump in. I’m playing with house money. I’m supposed to be a cab driver in Egypt. That’s the life I’m supposed to have.”
After college, he received a doctorate in public health while studying at Oxford, and then earned a medical degree at Columbia University, although he never practiced medicine. In his memoir, he writes that his decision to become a public-health official rather than a physician was made for him by meeting an alcoholic he calls Martha in New York City. She arrived in the ER with a head injury, and the attending doctor did not want to order a CT scan; El-Sayed advocated for her and found her a bed, keenly aware that she lacked insurance and that treating her would thus lose the hospital money. He secured antiretrovirals for her HIV and even found a rehab place for her—only for Martha to inform him that she would instead be going home with her daughter.
A few weeks later, he saw her lying face down on the subway: “As she turned her head, the lights went out on my clinical career.” Nothing he’d done in the hospital could have helped Martha, he concluded. The problem was the system.
In 2015, El-Sayed became executive director of the Detroit Health Department, where his proudest achievement was helping kids get free eye exams. Two years later, he launched his first bid for elected office—a long-shot campaign for governor of Michigan. He was hoping to capitalize on the young, anti-establishment energy that Sanders had recently generated in the Democratic presidential primary. To run his campaign, he tapped Millennial idealists who felt crushed by what they saw as the party establishment’s imposition of Hillary Clinton as the presidential nominee.
Brittany Huckabee’s documentary about the governor’s race was called How to Fix a Primary. The filmmaker spent more than a year traveling with El-Sayed and his team and watched as they learned the hard lessons of machine politics. In one scene, El-Sayed consoles his policy director, Rhiana Gunn-Wright—who would go on to be the architect of the Green New Deal—over the lack of support he is receiving compared with Gretchen Whitmer, the eventual winner. “Now you know why I have to be just, like, super thick-skinned and kind of mean sometimes,” he tells her. “Because inside, I’m really mushy, and it makes me sad that the world is what it is.”
The documentary showcases El-Sayed’s undoubted strengths: He can work a crowd, he can hone a line, he can land a joke, and he can deliver a speech that will move some audience members to tears. His anger at the various corrupt structures of American public life—Big Tech, Big Ag, Big Pharma, a health-care system that bankrupts people over medical debt, a political system in hock to megadonors—appears genuine. He also has a keen eye for populist issues that have been overlooked by the main parties. The first time I saw El-Sayed speak was from a makeshift plinth, a mile down a dead-end road in Saline Township, in eastern Michigan, where one of the country’s biggest data centers is being built. “Just look at it,” he told the small crowd, gesturing at the squat gray building behind him, his words underscored by the faint beeping of construction work. “Who governs this?”
The project, euphemistically called the Barn, has torn the local community apart. Town board meetings, once sleepy, have turned into bitter shouting matches, and local politicians have received death threats. “Look, nobody wanted this,” Saline’s lawyer, Fred Lucas, told me. More than 1,400 data centers were built or approved last year, according to Business Insider’s project tracker, and variations of the Barn dispute have occurred across rural America. In Louisiana, for example, Meta had had public officials sign nondisclosure agreements for the company’s proposed Hyperion data center. Legislators smuggled tax breaks into law in a bill about fiber-optic cables.
The speed with which public opinion has curdled against data centers is extraordinary—and that has become fertile territory for the Bernie faction, who harbor an innate suspicion of billionaires and their grand projects. Back in June, Whitmer happily posed with OpenAI’s Sam Altman at a groundbreaking ceremony for the Barn. “When Whitmer started pushing those really, really hard, I would just get calls from residents saying, Hey, can you help us too?” Robert Dube, the lawyer acting for the protesters in Saline, told me. El-Sayed has woven data-center opposition into his larger theme of the distorting power of corporate donations and the resultant rip-offs faced by ordinary Americans. The issue cuts across traditional party lines: About 70 percent of Americans do not want a data center in their area, according to polls. Belatedly, politicians across the spectrum are running away from data centers. The resistance to a proposed data center in Marshall, Michigan, “was made up of people who literally founded the Green Party of Michigan and some very Trump-supporting individuals,” Dube said.
At an event in the cornfield next to the Barn, a reporter asked El-Sayed whether taking money from Big Tech should be disqualifying for political candidates. “A corporation with interests in front of the government should not be able to pay money to help elect the people who are going to advance their interests,” he replied. “Economists call that rent-seeking. I think in politics we call that frank corruption.” Around him, locals held signs that read REAL BARNS NOT BRIBES. One woman wore a T-shirt offering to EAT THE RICH.
He discovered the strength of feeling against data centers the old-fashioned way, months before they became a campaign issue for other politicians. “I remember hearing about it in three town halls in a row in October,” he told me. “I’m like, we gotta move on this; this is one of those issues that you can see is just really, really freaking people out.” In recent weeks, he has also voiced concerns about the use of Flock cameras in law enforcement, an issue that unites reflexively anti-surveillance right-wingers and leftists who are suspicious about the power of the police. He gives a surprising amount of credit to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.—who criticizes junk food while also espousing a lot of unevidenced woo-woo. “The hard part about him is that he’s right about all the problems; he’s just wrong about all of the solutions,” El-Sayed said, adding: “Our food environment in America is trash. We eat ultra-processed food in large part because the big food corporations and Big Ag have colluded to figure out how to put a choke on our food environment, so we eat the least healthy things that make them the most money.”
El-Sayed’s advocacy for Medicare for All, another cherished cause of the Sanders faction, is a similar mixture of pragmatism and vibe-surfing. The slogan can mean many things, including the replacement of private health insurance with a single, government-run scheme.
Over the course of this campaign, El-Sayed has eased his previously dogmatic opposition to private health-care providers. What Medicare for All now means to him is a public guarantee, with transparent pricing and less of a cut going to middlemen. Thanks to his reputation as a left-wing street fighter, El-Sayed has managed to sell his base on a milder version of the policy.
This isn’t the only area in which he and other members of the Bernie Sanders Cinematic Universe have moved toward the center. Ben Krauss of the centrist think tank Searchlight Institute told me that El-Sayed “talked a lot about the Green New Deal” when he ran for Michigan governor in 2018. But today, as El-Sayed seeks to win over voters in the traditional center of the auto industry, mentions of climate change are far harder to find on his website. (El-Sayed told me that climate discussions have gotten hung up on wonkish stuff about “one and a half degrees or two degrees” of warming, and that he preferred to talk about how Americans “shouldn’t have to breathe unclean air or drink unclean water, and we deserve not to have to pay an arm and a leg.”) On the stump, El-Sayed has shaved his message down to a three-part refrain, which he is unashamed about repeating ad nauseam: “Money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for All.”
El-Sayed does not drink alcohol, but he did dabble with the great vice of the American left: Woke 1, as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez memorably described the peak phase of social-justice progressivism. Ahead of the primary, he scrubbed dozens of old YouTube videos, including one suggesting that Fourth of July fireworks “suck.” His campaign said they no longer represented his views; he told me that during the pandemic, some people became “internet-brained” and “sanctimonious,” and that “the excesses of that moment were a function of that moment.” He added that he was “not interested in defunding anything.”
El-Sayed is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, and he describes himself as a capitalist. These days, when he is asked about divisive cultural issues, he tries to pivot to affordability. When that fails, he falls back on conservative-friendly formulations such as Leave it to the states to decide and Health care should be between a patient and their doctor. “I don’t think people like to talk about it on the left, because they don’t want to say he’s moderating,” Krauss said. “And then no one wants to talk about it in the center, because they want him to moderate more.”
There is one issue on which El-Sayed’s positions have not moderated, however, and it is the one causing him the most grief: Israel.
In retrospect, the pool party was an error. On the day before the primary last month, El-Sayed attended a photoshoot next to a swimming pool, where he was pictured in his usual black V-neck and jeans, grinning alongside Hasan Piker. In another image, El-Sayed peered over his sunglasses, flanked by two women pointing finger guns at him. Cheesy? Yes. Tone-deaf, when he was about to squeak home by fewer than 15,000 votes? Also yes.
During the 10 days I spent in the Midwest ahead of the primary vote, Piker was everywhere. Without the streamer’s endorsement and appearances on the campaign trail, El-Sayed’s campaign might not have caught fire in the way that it did. In August 2025, the pair worked out together in Dearborn, on a livestream; El-Sayed—six years older and a head shorter—confidently corrected Piker’s form through kettlebell lifts and bench presses.
